  • (3/5) The agentialist and neo-expressivist accounts actually require the confabulation data to work: first-person authority is grounded not in transparent access but in the fact that avowals actively shape our psychology through self-interpretation, making the speaker's word authoritative because it becomes true through being sincerely uttered.

  • (2/5) First-person authority survives the interpretive turn not despite but because of confabulation: the authoritative self-ascriptions are precisely those where interpretation fails to get traction.
  • (2/5) First-person authority survives the interpretive turn not despite but because of confabulation: the authority consists in our being the source of the interpretation that gets socially ratified, not in getting our mental states right.
  • (3/5) Commitment to the interpretive turn commits one to denying that confabulation is ever strictly false self-ascription—what looks like confabulation is actually the imposition of a new interpretation that becomes true through adoption, making the phenomenon self-validating rather than self-deceiving.

U5. The agentialist and expressivist accounts collapse into the interpretive view they oppose: Moran's 'deliberative stance' and Bar-On's 'avowals' are themselves sophisticated forms of self-interpretation that presuppose rather than bypass the interpretive problem.

promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Moran's agentialist account and Bar-On's neo-expressivism, both of which claim to preserve first-person authority without appeal to observation or interpretation
Sketch

Moran says I know my belief by asking whether P rather than whether I believe P—shifting to a deliberative stance. But taking the deliberative stance is itself a complex interpretive achievement: I must identify which question is at issue, bracket various practical considerations, recognize that my conclusion commits me to a belief-ascription. Similarly, Bar-On's neo-expressivist avowals purport to be groundless expressions, but expressing requires knowing what mental state your utterance expresses—'I'm angry' expresses anger only if I've correctly interpreted my arousal as anger rather than fear or excitement. Both views try to bypass interpretation by invoking a more direct relation to mind, but that direct relation turns out to require the very interpretive capacity it was meant to replace. The views are unstable: they're covert forms of interpretationism that haven't recognized themselves as such.

Collapse argument is clever but interpretivists have responses; competent critical move without decisive reframing power.

  • (2/5) The agentialist solution (Moran) and interpretivist challenge (Carruthers) both fail because they presuppose a false dichotomy: that mental states are either reasons-responsive, making the deliberative stance appropriate, or they're causal posits, making the theoretical stance appropriate.

Interpretivism about self-knowledge commits its proponents to eliminativism about implicit attitudes: if we know our minds only through interpretation of behavior, and implicit attitudes are defined by their behavioral-contextual profile, then discovering one's implicit attitudes is just discovering how to correctly interpret one's behavior—but this collapses implicit attitudes into interpretive facts rather than psychological states.

Move · Target

Sketch

Interpretivists like Carruthers argue we access our own minds through the same interpretive mechanisms we use for others, reading off behavioral and contextual evidence. But this creates a dilemma for implicit attitudes (like implicit bias). Either implicit attitudes are psychological states prior to interpretation—in which case interpretivism is false, since these states exist independently of interpretive access—or implicit attitudes are themselves interpretive posits with no independent reality, making them mere patterns in interpretation rather than causes of behavior. The interpretivist can't have it both ways: treating implicit attitudes as discovered psychological facts while maintaining that self-knowledge is exhausted by interpretation. Schwitzgebel's skepticism about implicit attitudes may be the only consistent interpretivist position.

Dilemma for interpretivism about implicit attitudes is sharp but addresses a specific case rather than reframing the general debate.

U7. First-person authority and third-person epistemic advantage come apart: the interpretive turn shows that others often know our minds better while we retain practical authority over our self-ascriptions, and this bifurcation—not any unified 'first-person authority'—is what needs explaining.

promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — The shared assumption across the debate that first-person authority is a unified explanandum, whether one defends it (Moran, Bar-On) or explains it away (Carruthers)
Sketch

The debate assumes 'first-person authority' names a unified phenomenon. But the evidence supports bifurcation: therapists, spouses, and researchers often have better predictive and explanatory access to our mental states (epistemic advantage), while we retain a special authority to determine what attitudes we'll be held to (practical/normative authority). The confabulation literature shows others' epistemic advantage; the persistence of first-person asymmetry in conversation shows our practical authority. These are different phenomena with different grounds: epistemic advantage comes from better interpretive position and evidence; practical authority comes from our role as agents who can be held responsible only for attitudes we acknowledge. Trying to explain 'first-person authority' as a unified thing generates pseudo-problems. The real question is why we retain practical authority despite lacking epistemic advantage.

Appraiser (blind)
Bifurcation of epistemic and practical authority is useful but doesn't resolve the underlying tensions.

U8. The confabulation literature shows not that we lack first-person authority but that first-person authority extends only to synchronic rational relations, not to the causal-historical genealogy of our states.

promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Schwitzgebel and others who treat confabulation cases as globally undermining first-person authority
Sketch

Nisbett-Wilson cases involve subjects misidentifying the causes of their judgments, not misidentifying what they currently believe or value. We confabulate about the 'because' but not about the 'what' or 'that.' First-person authority was never supposed to cover psychological etiology—Freud already taught us we're opaque to our own causal history. What we have authority about is the rational space: which commitments we'll stand by, what follows from what in our view, what coheres with what. I can be authoritative that I prefer this job because of its location even when the real cause was anchoring bias, because the authority concerns my current rational endorsement, not causal history. The interpretive turn threatens first-person authority only if we conflate two different dimensions of self-knowledge. The key premise is that rational-space relations are constitutively accessible to the subject in a way causal-historical facts are not.

Appraiser (blind)
Rational-space versus causal-history distinction limits confabulation's threat but the move is somewhat familiar from replies to skepticism.
Merged in (2)
  • (3/5) The confabulation literature shows that first-person authority is doxastic—it's authority about what I believe, not authority that what I believe is correct—and this distinction has been systematically conflated in the debate.
  • (3/5) First-person authority is not authority about what attitudes you have but authority about what attitude-report to endorse, and the confabulation literature systematically confuses these two different domains of authority.

U9. Agentialist and interpretivist accounts are not rivals but describe different stages of a single process: interpretation generates candidate self-ascriptions, and agential endorsement selects among them, with authority attaching only to the latter.

Move · Target
reframing — The assumption that Moran's agentialism and Carruthers's interpretivism are competing explanations rather than complementary stages
Sketch

The debate presupposes we must choose between interpretation (Carruthers) and agency (Moran) as the basis of self-knowledge. But actual self-knowledge involves both sequentially. We do interpret ourselves from behavioral and contextual evidence, generating multiple possible readings of what we think or want—this explains the empirical findings. But then we must decide which interpretation to endorse going forward, and this endorsement is an agential act that carries first-person authority. When you ask what I believe about free will, I might recognize evidence for multiple conflicting interpretations of my utterances and behaviors; my authority consists not in detecting which interpretation is correct but in deciding which to stand behind. The key premise is that self-knowledge requires ratification, not just generation, of self-interpretations. This makes authority compatible with interpretive opacity.

Appraiser (blind)
Two-stage model reconciling positions is constructive but may not satisfy either camp that their view captures what matters.

Move · Target
commitment — Carruthers and Gopnik's symmetry thesis—that self-interpretation uses the same evidence-base as other-interpretation, just more conveniently accessed.
Sketch

Interpretivists like Carruthers argue we read ourselves behaviourally like we read others, but they're committed to the claim that all evidence available for self-interpretation is symmetrically available for other-interpretation (modulo practical access). This commitment is false. When I interpret my behaviour, I have access to how considerations phenomenologically struck me—which considerations felt weighty, which I experienced as reasons. You interpreting me must theorize about what reasons moved me; I can consult how reasons felt. This isn't non-interpretive access to beliefs themselves (so it grants the interpretive turn), but it's an interpretive asymmetry that explains authority. The key premise: phenomenology of deliberation—the experienced weight of reasons—is both (a) genuinely phenomenal/experiential, not requiring interpretation, and (b) evidentially relevant to what I believe, since beliefs are constitutively connected to dispositions to treat considerations as reasons with particular weights.

The phenomenology-of-reasons asymmetry is interesting but the evidential advantage claim needs more work to distinguish from observational models.

Move · Target

Moran argues we know our beliefs not by observation but by answering the world-directed question (asking whether P, not whether I believe P). This is supposed to preserve authority while acknowledging we don't merely observe our beliefs. But if I determine what I believe by rational deliberation about P, this should eliminate the very interpretive uncertainty that motivates the debate—I should be able to make my beliefs determinate simply by deliberating. The fact that we often remain genuinely uncertain about our beliefs (not just what's true, but what WE believe) shows that agentialism either (a) collapses back into observationalism (deliberation reveals rather than constitutes belief), or (b) can't explain residual uncertainty without abandoning the claim that deliberative self-constitution grounds authority. The key premise: genuine cases of interpretive self-uncertainty (do I really believe in God? Am I truly committed to this relationship?) are incompatible with the claim that I settle what I believe through deliberation about the world-directed question.

The uncertainty objection to Moran is sharp and publishable but represents internal critique rather than reframing the debate.

Interpretivists like Carruthers claim confabulation shows we infer our attitudes from behavioral evidence. If interpretation (whether observational or behavioral-inferential) requires an independently existing interpretandum, then confabulation cases where there's nothing determinate to interpret undermine interpretation just as much as observation. Both models share the assumption that attitudes are standing states we discover. The key premise: systematic confabulation is better explained by attitude-generation than by bad attitude-detection. This reveals that the observation vs. interpretation debate rests on a shared false presupposition.

The attitude-generation view is interesting but already present in the literature; showing it undermines both models equally is competent but incremental.

U13. First-person authority survives interpretation not because self-knowledge is privileged access but because self-constitution is privileged action: the interpretive process itself has different causal powers when directed at oneself.

Move · Target
distinction — Both pure interpretivists like Carruthers who treat self and other-interpretation as symmetrical, and agentialists like Moran who ground authority in a non-interpretive deliberative stance
Sketch

The distinction is between epistemic privilege (better access to pre-existing facts) and constitutive privilege (special power to make things true). When I interpret myself as believing P, this interpretation doesn't merely report a belief—it can consolidate, crystallize, or even bring into being a determinate belief where only proto-attitudes existed. This differs from interpreting others precisely because my self-interpretation enters the causal loop that produces my mental states. The argument turns on accepting that many mental states are indeterminate or inchoate until articulated, and that self-interpretation plays a constitutive role in this articulation. This explains why I'm authoritative about my beliefs even if I arrive at them interpretively: not because I observe them better, but because my saying-so partly makes-them-so. The asymmetry between self and other-ascription is thus grounded in differential constitutive power, not differential epistemic access.

The constitutive privilege idea overlaps significantly with thesis 0; this version adds causal-loop details but doesn't clearly advance beyond it.

Accepting interpretivism commits you to rejecting the synchronic unity of mind: if propositional attitudes are interpretive constructions rather than detected facts, then there is no fact about whether beliefs attributed at different times or by different interpretive schemes belong to a single mind.

Move · Target
commitment — Carruthers and Gopnik-style interpretivists who help themselves to ordinary assumptions about personal identity while treating mental states as interpretive constructions

Interpretivists like Carruthers treat propositional attitudes as the outputs of interpretation—useful posits that organize behavior. But interpretation is always relative to an interpretive scheme and purpose. Different schemes (folk psychology, various subpersonal theories, psychoanalytic interpretation) carve behavior into different belief-sets. The key premise is that without observer-independent mental facts, there's no principled basis for saying which interpretive scheme tracks the 'real' unity of a mind over time or at a time. We lose the unity that makes 'my mind' a coherent subject of self-knowledge. Interpretivists who want to preserve talk of 'what I really believe' must covertly reintroduce the observer-independent facts they officially reject. They cannot consistently be both interpretivists and realists about personal identity or mental unity.

The unity-of-mind challenge to interpretivism is philosophically serious but may be too broad a consequence to establish convincingly.

If interpretation grounds self-knowledge but we retain first-person authority, then authority cannot reduce to having better evidence (since ex hypothesi self- and other-interpretation can rely on the same evidence base). The authority must instead arise from features like: practised skill, holistic constraints, or stakes in getting it right. But this conception of authority—authority as interpretive expertise rather than observational privilege—is one that defenders of first-person authority typically reject because it makes the authority seem merely pragmatic or conventional. The argument shows that neo-expressivists like Bar-On and agentialists like Moran cannot both embrace the interpretive turn and maintain that first-person authority is a distinctive epistemic kind. The key premise is that if two interpreters have access to the same evidence, any remaining asymmetry must be non-evidential.

Identifying that interpretive authority undermines evidentialist assumptions is valuable but the argument needs tightening to show both sides actually rely on evidentialism.

Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption that motivated reasoning and interpretive bias undermine rather than constitute first-person authority
Sketch

The standard view treats motivated reasoning as undermining self-knowledge—if I'm biased in self-interpretation, I lack the authority I thought I had. But this gets it backwards. When you attribute a belief to me, you're uncertain both about my mental states and about which interpretive biases I'm deploying in reading myself. When I attribute a belief to myself, even if I'm deploying motivated reasoning, I'm authoritative about which motivated construal I'm committed to. The asymmetry isn't about better access to mental states but about direct access to my own interpretive stance. Your interpretation of me requires a second-order interpretation (reading my self-reading), while my self-interpretation is simply first-order commitment to an interpretation. This reframes the debate: both sides are right that self-knowledge is interpretive and that authority exists, but the authority is about interpretive commitment rather than about pre-interpretive mental states.

Appraiser (blind)
Interesting inversion but the payoff—authority about interpretive stance—seems too narrow to resolve the debate.

U17. First-person authority for avowals is preserved under interpretation because self-ascriptions are answer-resistant: the attempt to verify 'I believe P' by gathering evidence itself alters what I believe about P.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Interpretivist accounts like Carruthers and Gopnik that assimilate first- and third-person epistemic positions
Sketch

The debate assumes that if self-knowledge is interpretive, then first- and third-person methods converge, eliminating asymmetry. But this ignores a distinctive feature of self-interpretation: the measurement problem. When I try to interpret whether I believe P by examining my behavior and circumstances, this very examination constitutes a form of deliberation about P that changes my belief state. The key premise is that mental states, unlike external facts, are affected by the investigative process itself in the first-person case but not the third-person case. When you interpret whether I believe P, your interpretation doesn't alter my belief; when I interpret whether I believe P, the process of marshaling evidence about P necessarily engages my belief-forming mechanisms about P. This is why simply asking myself 'Do I believe P?' leads naturally into asking 'Is P true?'—they're not alternative methods but inseparable for the self-interpreter. This answer-resistance grounds an ineliminable asymmetry even if both involve interpretation.

Appraiser (blind)
Measurement problem for self-interpretation is interesting but the practical significance is limited.

U18. First-person authority and confabulation are both explained by a metacognitive prediction mechanism: we have privileged access to our own predictive models of our behaviour, not to the behaviour itself.

Sketch

Both observationalists and interpretivists assume self-knowledge is retrospective—we look at what we did/thought and report it. But what if self-ascription draws on the forward models we use to predict and control our own behaviour? On this view, when you report your intention, you're reporting your system's prediction about what it will do, which is typically accurate (hence authority) but can dissociate from actual processes (hence confabulation). This isn't interpretation (it's not evidence-based inference from behaviour) but isn't observation either (you're accessing the model, not the modeled). It explains the phenomenology of immediacy while accommodating systematic error. The asymmetry arises because you have access to your own predictive machinery but not others'. The key premise is that introspection taps into motor control and action planning systems rather than belief-monitoring systems.

Appraiser (blind)
Predictive processing angle is timely and explains some phenomena, but similar proposals exist and the forward-model story needs more work to distinguish from interpretation.

U19. The debate falsely assumes interpretation and direct access are competing explanations, when actually confabulation cases show that first-person authority exists even when first-person accuracy fails—we have authority to be wrong about ourselves in a way we lack authority to be wrong about others.

Move · Target
counterexample — The shared assumption that accuracy and authority go together, held by both observationalists (who ground authority in accurate access) and interpretivists (who deny authority because access is inaccurate)
Sketch

In Nisbett and Wilson's studies, subjects confabulate explanations for their choices, but their confabulations are treated as authoritative—psychologists don't correct them ('No, you actually chose that because of position effects'). When you sincerely self-ascribe a belief wrongly, we accommodate this by saying 'You're confused about what you believe' rather than simply 'You're wrong and here's what you really believe.' This authority-without-accuracy is the real first-person asymmetry. It cannot be explained by either direct access (which would ensure accuracy) or by pure interpretivism (which would make sincere self-ascriptions just another fallible interpretation to be weighed against behavioral evidence). The key premise is that first-person authority is normative authority over what counts as the explanandum—your sincere self-ascription determines what needs explaining—not epistemic authority about the explanation. Confabulation doesn't undermine this authority; it exemplifies it.

Appraiser (blind)
Authority-without-accuracy is interesting but the normative vs epistemic split is familiar.

U20. The interpretive and observational models both fail because they treat introspection as discovery of standing states, but most psychological self-knowledge is knowledge of dispositions, and knowing your own dispositions is predictive rather than observational—you have authority because you can make yourself predictable, not because you observe yourself better.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption that beliefs are categorical states and that self-knowledge requires detecting which state you're in, held by classical perceptualists and interpretivists alike
Sketch

Both the perceptual model (I observe that I believe P) and the interpretive model (I infer from my behavior that I believe P) assume that to know I believe P is to detect a categorical state I'm currently in. But beliefs are better understood as dispositions to judge, assert, and act in certain ways. The key premise: first-person knowledge of dispositions works differently than third-person knowledge—not because you observe the disposition's basis better, but because you can normally make yourself manifest the disposition on demand (you can bring the belief to consciousness, rehearse it, commit to acting on it). This self-predictability gives you a kind of authority: you can guarantee certain predictions about what you'll judge or say in a way others can't, not by observation but by agential control over the disposition's manifestation. This explains authority without requiring transparent access, and accommodates interpretation (you might need behavioral evidence for some dispositions) while preserving asymmetry (you can control manifestation in ways others can't).

Appraiser (blind)
Self-predictability through agential control is interesting but the dispositional account needs development.

U21. First-person authority exists only for those mental states we are currently forming through deliberation, not for standing attitudes or emotional states we discover.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
distinction — Both expressivist accounts (Bar-On) and interpretive accounts (Carruthers) that assume first-person authority must have a unified source
Sketch

The debate treats 'first-person authority' as a unified phenomenon requiring a unified explanation. But Moran's agentialist account actually only explains authority over attitudes formed through rational deliberation (what to believe, intend, or value), while confabulation cases concern pre-existing emotions, implicit biases, and motivations we discover rather than form. When I ask 'Do I believe P?' in deliberative mode, I'm not discovering but deciding—the question is transparent to 'Is P true?' This explains why authority exists for some self-ascriptions but not others without requiring either pure observation or pure interpretation. The key premise is that deliberative and archaeological self-knowledge are fundamentally different epistemic projects with different accuracy conditions.

Appraiser (blind)
Restricting authority to deliberatively-formed attitudes is already Moran's position, not an advance on it.

U22. Interpretive theories are committed to treating confabulation as systematically false belief, but confabulators actually express genuine attitudes they have—toward justification and self-presentation—just not the attitudes they think they're expressing.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Carruthers and other interpretivists who use confabulation as evidence against first-person authority
Sketch

When Nisbett and Wilson's subjects confabulate reasons for choosing stockings, interpretivists treat this as false belief about mental causation. But the confabulation expresses something true: the subject's commitment to certain kinds of justification, their standards for what counts as a good reason, their self-concept. The subject isn't mistaken about having a mental state—they're correctly expressing their evaluative stance while being wrong about which mental state prompted the original action. This means interpretation gets self-knowledge right more often than confabulation literature suggests, but it succeeds by expressing different (higher-order, normative) attitudes than subjects intend. The key premise is that expressivism is right that first-person avowal expresses rather than reports, but what gets expressed includes normative and justificatory attitudes the subject actually has.

Appraiser (blind)
Confabulation expressing different (normative) attitudes is clever but limited payoff.

U23. First-person authority survives interpretation because self-interpretation operates under constitutive rational constraints that other-interpretation doesn't face: gross self-misinterpretation makes the interpreter irrational in a way that misinterpreting others doesn't.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption between Carruthers and Gopnik that interpretive symmetry entails epistemic symmetry
Sketch

The debate assumes that if self-knowledge is interpretive, it must be epistemically symmetric with other-knowledge. But self-interpretation is subject to rational norms that constrain interpretation from within. If I conclude through interpretation that I don't care about my child's welfare, while continuing to act solicitously, I face rational pressure to revise either the interpretation or my behavior in ways that someone interpreting me from outside doesn't face. This isn't epistemic privilege but constitutive pressure: my self-interpretation partially constitutes what attitudes I rationally can be said to have. The asymmetry isn't about access but about the rational standing of the interpreter. The key premise is that rationality requires a kind of self-knowledge that is presupposed by, not derived from, third-personal interpretation.

Appraiser (blind)
Rational constraints on self-interpretation creating asymmetry is well-trodden ground.

U24. The agentialist position collapses into interpretivism once we recognize that deliberative transparency itself requires interpretation of what counts as a reason.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Moran's agentialist account claiming to avoid the interpretive turn
Sketch

Moran claims that answering 'Do I believe P?' through deliberating about whether P is true avoids interpretation. But deliberation requires determining what counts as evidence for P, which requires understanding one's epistemic standards, background beliefs, and inferential dispositions—all of which require interpretation. When I reason from 'P' to 'I believe P,' the transparency move obscures that I must interpret my own epistemic framework to determine whether my consideration of P's truth constitutes believing it or merely entertaining it. Even the agentialist must interpret their own rational-agent-role-occupancy. The key premise is that there is no uninterpreted access to one's own rational processes, because recognizing something as a reason requires situating it within an interpreted framework of one's commitments.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim that deliberation requires interpretation has been made before; this restates a familiar criticism of Moran without sufficient new leverage.

U25. The confabulation literature actually supports rather than undermines first-person authority, because confabulation itself is a distinctively first-personal capacity unavailable in third-person attribution.

promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — The standard interpretation of confabulation studies (Schwitzgebel, Carruthers) as straightforwardly undermining first-person authority.
Sketch

Nisbett and Wilson are typically read as showing we lack introspective access. But confabulation requires more than mere misattribution—it requires generating rationalizations that feel like reasons to the subject, that integrate into a first-personal narrative in a way that third-person hypotheses don't. When I confabulate about why I chose these stockings, I'm not merely guessing; I'm producing a candidate reason that has a particular phenomenological and normative grip on me. This capacity to generate reasons that feel like my reasons (even when they aren't) is itself a form of first-person authority—authority over the space of reasons I can occupy, if not over the causes of my behavior. The asymmetry persists: you can hypothesize reasons for my action, but you cannot confabulate for me.

Appraiser (blind)
Clever inversion but the payoff is limited—showing confabulation itself requires first-person capacities doesn't rescue first-person authority in the contested domain.

U26. First-person authority consists not in privileged access to mental states but in constitutive control over which interpretations of oneself become true.

Move · Target
reframing — Both sides of the debate—those defending epistemic first-person authority (Moran) and those reducing self-knowledge to third-personal interpretation (Carruthers, Gopnik)—share the assumption that authority must be epistemic.
Sketch

The debate assumes first-person authority requires epistemic privilege—better evidence, more direct access. But authority can be practical rather than epistemic. When I sincerely avow a belief or intention, I'm not reporting a pre-existing fact I'm best positioned to observe; I'm making it the case that this interpretation is correct by committing to it. The key premise: self-interpretation has world-to-mind direction of fit for rational agents. My sincere avowals don't describe my mental states, they constitute their rational identity by creating commitments I'm then accountable to. This explains the asymmetry: others can predict my behaviour, but only I can bind myself to an interpretation and thereby make it authoritative. The interpretive turn is right that we construct self-knowledge, wrong only in assuming construction must be epistemic rather than practical.

Appraiser (blind)
Practical authority through commitment is already a recognized position in the literature; this restates it without sufficient novelty.

U27. First-person authority requires interpretive dependency: only by being hostage to others' reactions can my self-ascriptions have the kind of authority they do.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
instability — Moran and Bar-On's attempts to ground first-person authority in non-interpretive resources (deliberative stance, expressive vehicle) independent of third-personal assessment.
Sketch

Accounts defending first-person authority (Moran, Bar-On) against interpretivism try to ground it in something internal—agential commitment, expressive directness. But this move is unstable: what makes a self-ascription authoritative rather than merely insistent is that it creates legitimate expectations in others, which requires that the practice of granting authority serves social coordination. The key premise: authority is a status others must recognize, not a metaphysical fact about access. Trying to ground first-person authority independently of third-personal interpretive practices collapses—the authority exists only within the practice of generally deferring to sincere self-ascription. This reveals that defenders of first-person authority are committed to the very interpretive social framework they oppose. The asymmetry between self and other-ascription is real but is a social achievement, not a consequence of inner access or agential magic.

Appraiser (blind)
Showing first-person authority depends on social recognition is not new; this makes the point clearly but without advancing beyond existing social-practice accounts.

U28. The confabulation literature and first-person authority target different mental state types: confabulation occurs for sub-personal states that never had first-person authority, while we retain authority over personal-level commitments that are constituted by avowability.

Move · Target
reframing — Both sides' assumption that confabulation about mental states and first-person authority concern the same ontological category
Sketch

Nisbett & Wilson show subjects confabulate about implicit preferences and automatic processes. But these were never candidates for first-person authority in the philosophically relevant sense—they're not the attitudes that figure in rational explanation and criticism. When I sincerely avow 'I believe abortion is permissible,' I'm not reporting an inner state but taking a stand, entering a commitment into my rational economy. This act is self-verifying: my genuine avowal makes it true that this belief figures in my personal-level psychology, even if implicit attitude tests or my behavioral evidence suggest otherwise. The appearance of conflict between empirical psychology and first-person authority dissolves: they study different psychological kinds. The key premise: personal-level attitudes are those individuated by their role in reason-giving, and avowal is constitutive of, not evidence for, such attitudes.

Appraiser (blind)
The personal/subpersonal distinction is standard; applying it here dissolves rather than engages the debate.

U29. First-person authority is an illusion produced by confirmation bias in the interpretation process: we accept interpretations of ourselves at lower evidential thresholds than interpretations of others, creating spurious asymmetry.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — Moran and Bar-On's assumption that the authority asymmetry is a datum to be explained rather than itself an artifact of the phenomena the interpretivists identified
Sketch

Both camps assume the authority asymmetry is real and needs explaining, but the confabulation literature suggests a simpler hypothesis: we're bad at interpreting ourselves and don't realize it because we apply motivated reasoning. When interpreting others, social correction forces higher evidential standards; when interpreting ourselves, confirmation bias runs unchecked. What Bar-On and Moran treat as authority is actually overconfidence plus the fact that others rarely challenge our self-reports. Schwitzgebel's cases of disagreement about one's own experiences show this: people resist revising self-interpretations not because they have authority but because they have bias. This predicts what we see: the appearance of authority is strongest precisely where checking is hardest (phenomenal states, intentions) and weakest where evidence is public (skills, personality traits). First-person authority is the self-serving interpretation of our own incompetence at self-interpretation.

Appraiser (blind)
The confirmation-bias debunking is psychologically plausible but doesn't engage the normative dimension of authority; similar deflationary moves have been made.

U30. First-person authority is parasitic on other-person vulnerability: we have authority about our own minds only in domains where others can be systematically fooled about theirs.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
reframing — Both access and interpretivist theorists who seek positive grounds for first-person authority
Sketch

Both sides assume first-person authority is about the self-other asymmetry in getting mental states right. But the real pattern is this: first-person authority exists only for mental state types where third-person attribution is especially unreliable—precisely where behavioural evidence is defeatable and where confabulation is possible. I have authority about my occurrent thoughts because you cannot reliably infer them from my behaviour; I lack authority about my implicit attitudes because behavioral evidence constrains both of us equally. First-person authority is thus not a special epistemic position but rather the flipside of third-person epistemic limitation. The asymmetry doesn't need grounding in access or agentialism; it's grounded in the differential reliability of evidence sources across mental state types. The debate has been looking for a positive story about first-person capacities when the explanation is negative, about third-person incapacities.

Appraiser (blind)
Negative explanation via third-person limitations is clever but the asymmetry still requires positive account of why self-access differs.

U31. Agentialist accounts like Moran's that ground first-person authority in rational self-constitution are committed to denying first-person authority to anyone who forms attitudes non-rationally, revealing the view's unacceptable elitism.

Scores
promise 2/5 · residual –/5 · worst –/5 · unattacked
Move · Target
commitment — Moran's agentialist account and similar rational-constitution views
Sketch

Moran grounds first-person authority in the stance of deliberative agency: I know my belief by deciding what to believe rather than observing what I already believe. This commits him to the view that first-person authority varies with rational capacity and the exercise of deliberative agency. But this means children, the severely depressed, the akratic, and anyone forming attitudes through non-rational means lack first-person authority about those attitudes—they must adopt the third-person, observational stance Moran reserves for others. This is not merely counterintuitive but contradicts the phenomenology: even in akrasia, I seem to have first-person authority about both the rational belief I should hold and the contrary attitude I actually hold. The key premise is that if authority is grounded in a capacity, those lacking the capacity lack the authority, and Moran cannot restrict his account to 'ideally rational' agents without abandoning the explanatory project.

Appraiser (blind)
The elitism objection to Moran is familiar; he has responses about the scope of deliberative stance availability.
